logline: First-generation Egyptian-American Ramy Hassan pursues spiritual meaning and romantic satisfaction in suburban New Jersey, caught between his Muslim faith and the pull of millennial American life - a semi-autobiographical Hulu comedy that made Ramy Youssef one of television's most distinctive voices.

renewal.note: Ramy concluded with Season 3 on September 30, 2022. Hulu did not renew for a fourth season. Creator Ramy Youssef indicated in 2024 he remained open to continuing the story.

bollymeter.basis: 98% on Rotten Tomatoes. Metacritic awarded an 84 from 36 critics. RogerEbert.com gave a perfect score, calling Ramy 'unlike anything else on television.' Hollywood Reporter praised it as 'extremely funny, unexpectedly emotional and consistently eye-opening.'

pull_quotes.text: Ramy is unlike anything else on television, but its closest relative is Better Call Saul.
Extremely funny, unexpectedly emotional and consistently eye-opening with a confident voice.

seasons.review_body: Ramy's first season arrived in April 2019 as one of the most unexpected critical sensations of the year, scoring 98% on Rotten Tomatoes and an 84 Metascore from 36 critics. The show's originality lay in its refusal to make a simple argument about Muslim-American identity. Ramy Hassan is morally inconsistent, spiritually sincere, and often selfish in ways that television rarely permits characters coded as representatives of a marginalised community. IndieWire praised how the series 'treats its characters' lives with the utmost compassion.' TV Guide singled out the portrayal of the Hassan family as 'a portrait of an American Muslim family never before seen in a sitcom, because these kinds of characters are never allowed to be this complicated.' Variety credited the show's success to 'the specificity of its star's perspective and experience.'

episode_reviews.title: Feelings
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The pilot introduces Ramy Hassan as a young man who prays five times a day and also lies to women about his name on dating apps - a comedy of sincere hypocrisy rather than simple contradiction. The New Jersey suburb is rendered with complete specificity, and Youssef's performance is immediately compelling.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Ramy attempting to reconcile his religious devotion with a decision that directly contradicts it - the show's central irresolvable tension stated without judgment.

critic_note.text: A portrait of an American Muslim family never before seen in a sitcom - these characters are never allowed to be this complicated.

bollymeter.basis: 95% on Rotten Tomatoes. The season added Mahershala Ali as Sheikh Ali Hassan and earned broad acclaim for deepening Ramy's spiritual crisis through a mentor relationship built on genuine complexity rather than easy resolution.

seasons.review_body: Season 2 maintained the show's near-perfect critical standing at 95% on Rotten Tomatoes while significantly expanding its emotional register. The addition of Mahershala Ali as Sheikh Ali Hassan gave Ramy's spiritual search a foil of genuine moral weight - a Muslim authority figure who is neither a cartoon nor an uncomplicated hero. The season deepened the father-son dynamics of the Hassan family and continued the show's formal experiments, including an episode dedicated entirely to May Calamawy's Dena that stands as one of the year's best half-hours of television. The season's final stretch is the show's most dramatically powerful to date.
seasons.season_over_season: Season 2 expands the show's moral universe with Mahershala Ali's Sheikh, deepening the spiritual search at the show's centre into something more dramatically charged and more honestly complicated.

bollymeter.basis: 92% on Rotten Tomatoes. Critics found the final season solid if slightly less revelatory than its predecessors, with Ramy's character arc reaching conclusions that divided viewers who had invested in his spiritual journey.

seasons.review_body: The third and final season of Ramy earned 92% on Rotten Tomatoes - a slight decline from the near-perfect scores of its predecessors but still solid. The season picks up after the dramatic rupture at the end of Season 2, with Ramy navigating the consequences of his choices with the same uncomfortable mix of self-awareness and self-sabotage that defined the character from the start. The ending reads as inconclusive rather than deliberately open - a function of the show's cancellation cutting off a story that had not reached its natural resolution. For devotees of the series, the third season is unmissable; newcomers are better served starting from the beginning.
seasons.season_over_season: Season 3 continues the show's honest portrait of spiritual struggle but arrives under the shadow of an unplanned ending - stronger as character study than as narrative conclusion.
